misconceptions.statement: Rubbing creates electricity out of nothing, like making heat.
misconceptions.why: Students see the effect appear only after rubbing, so they think rubbing makes it.
misconceptions.fix: Rubbing does not make charge. It moves charge that was already in the materials from one object to the other.

probe.question: Where does the charge on a rubbed comb come from?
probe.wrong_answer: It is newly made by the rubbing.

misconceptions.root_belief: an effect appearing means it was newly created
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about charge conservation and charging by friction

misconceptions.statement: Rubbing makes the comb hot and the heat makes it attract paper.
misconceptions.why: Rubbing is linked to warmth in everyday experience.
misconceptions.fix: Attraction is caused by electric charge gained by the comb, not by heat.

probe.question: Why does a rubbed comb pick up paper bits?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the rubbing made it warm.

misconceptions.root_belief: familiar effect of an action explains every outcome

misconceptions.statement: Any two objects become charged if you rub them, even two pieces of the same plastic scale.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralise from combs and balloons to every material.
misconceptions.fix: Charging by rubbing works well only for certain insulating materials, and the pairing matters. A metal held in the hand cannot hold the charge.

probe.question: Will rubbing a steel spoon held in your hand make it attract paper?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, any rubbed object will attract paper.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule seen once works for everything

misconceptions.statement: Only the object that is rubbed gets charged, the cloth does not.
misconceptions.why: Attention is on the comb or rod, so the rubbing cloth is ignored.
misconceptions.fix: Both objects get charged, with opposite kinds of charge.

probe.question: A glass rod is rubbed with silk. Which object is charged?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the glass rod.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the thing you watch is affected
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about electrostatics and charging by friction

misconceptions.statement: Positive charge moves from one object to the other when rubbed.
misconceptions.why: Students think positive is the active charge, and the object with positive charge seems to have gained something.
misconceptions.fix: In solids it is the negative charges (electrons) that move. An object becomes positive by losing them.

probe.question: When glass is rubbed with silk and becomes positive, what moved?
probe.wrong_answer: Positive charge moved from silk to glass.

misconceptions.root_belief: the thing gained is what moved
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of secondary students' models of electrons and charging

misconceptions.statement: The charge on a rubbed object disappears into nothing when it is discharged.
misconceptions.why: The attraction vanishes so students think the charge is destroyed.
misconceptions.fix: Charge is never destroyed. It flows away to the ground or neutralises opposite charge.

probe.question: A charged rod is touched to the earth and stops attracting paper. What happened to its charge?
probe.wrong_answer: It was destroyed.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: misconception research on conservation of charge

misconceptions.statement: Rubbing gives both objects the same kind of charge.
misconceptions.why: Students expect the same action to have the same result on both objects.
misconceptions.fix: One object gains electrons and becomes negative, while the other loses them and becomes positive, in equal amounts.

probe.question: A balloon is rubbed on hair. What charges do the balloon and hair have?
probe.wrong_answer: Both are negative.

misconceptions.root_belief: same action gives same result everywhere

misconceptions.statement: A charged object attracts only objects with opposite charge, so paper must be charged.
misconceptions.why: Students apply 'unlike attract' to every case of attraction.
misconceptions.fix: A charged object also attracts neutral objects by causing a slight separation of charge in them.

probe.question: Why does a charged comb attract uncharged paper bits?
probe.wrong_answer: The paper must already have opposite charge.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on polarisation and attraction of neutral objects

misconceptions.statement: The paper bits are attracted because they are light, not because of charge.
misconceptions.why: Students think light things are pulled by any invisible force or air movement.
misconceptions.fix: The attraction is an electric force. A comb that is not charged will not lift the same bits.

probe.question: A dry comb that has not been rubbed is held near paper bits. Will they be lifted because they are light?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, light paper is always lifted.

misconceptions.root_belief: one obvious property is the only cause

misconceptions.statement: An uncharged object has no charges at all in it.
misconceptions.why: The word uncharged is read as empty of charge.
misconceptions.fix: A neutral object has equal amounts of positive and negative charge that cancel out.

probe.question: Does a neutral piece of paper contain any charges?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it contains no charge.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas on neutral objects and atoms

misconceptions.statement: Positive charge is the stronger charge and negative means no charge or lack of it.
misconceptions.why: Positive and negative are read as 'more' and 'less' in number sense.
misconceptions.fix: Both are equally real kinds of charge. Negative is not absence of charge, it is the opposite kind.

probe.question: A rod has negative charge. How much charge does it have compared to a neutral rod?
probe.wrong_answer: Less, since negative means less.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Two negatively charged objects attract each other because they are both full of charge.
misconceptions.why: Students think similar things pull together like friends.
misconceptions.fix: Like charges push each other away, whether both are positive or both negative.

probe.question: Two balloons are rubbed on hair and hung close together. What happens?
probe.wrong_answer: They attract each other.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar things go together

misconceptions.statement: Opposite charges attract only if they are exactly equal in amount.
misconceptions.why: Students bring in whole-number ideas of balancing.
misconceptions.fix: Unlike charges attract each other whatever the amounts. The size only changes how strong the pull is.

probe.question: A strongly charged positive rod is near a weakly charged negative ball. Do they attract?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only if amounts are equal.

misconceptions.root_belief: balance or equality is needed for any effect

misconceptions.statement: If an object is attracted to a charged rod, it must be charged.
misconceptions.why: Attraction seems proof of opposite charge.
misconceptions.fix: Attraction can also happen with a neutral object. Only repulsion proves that an object is charged.

probe.question: A balloon is attracted to a charged rod. Is the balloon surely charged?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it must be charged.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student reasoning about electrostatic attraction and repulsion tests

misconceptions.statement: The electroscope leaves separate because the charge makes them heavy and they hang apart.
misconceptions.why: Students link charge with weight or pull downward.
misconceptions.fix: The leaves get the same charge, so they repel each other and spread apart.

probe.question: Why do the two foil leaves of a charged electroscope spread?
probe.wrong_answer: The charge makes them heavy and they fall apart.

misconceptions.root_belief: more stuff means heavier and pulled down

misconceptions.statement: An electroscope tells you whether the charge is positive or negative.
misconceptions.why: Students think a visible effect must show every property.
misconceptions.fix: A simple electroscope only shows that charge is present. It cannot tell the kind of charge.

probe.question: The leaves of an electroscope open on touching a rod. Is the rod positive?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, opening shows positive.

misconceptions.root_belief: a visible effect shows all properties

misconceptions.statement: Charge cannot pass through metals, which is why metals are not charged.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the electrical behaviour of metals with their usual hardness or heat behaviour.
misconceptions.fix: Metals let charge move easily, so they can be charged but lose it quickly through the hand.

probe.question: Why does a metal rod held in the hand not stay charged?
probe.wrong_answer: Metals do not let charge pass.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Earthing removes charge by making the object cold or by absorbing it like a sponge.
misconceptions.why: Students picture the ground as soaking things up.
misconceptions.fix: The ground is a huge conductor, so charge flows between the object and the earth until the object is neutral.

probe.question: How does touching a charged rod to the earth discharge it?
probe.wrong_answer: The earth soaks up the charge like a sponge.

misconceptions.root_belief: unfamiliar processes work like everyday objects

misconceptions.statement: A spark from a sweater is made by friction heating the air.
misconceptions.why: Rubbing is associated with heat and fire.
misconceptions.fix: The spark is charge jumping through the air in a sudden discharge, heating the air only briefly.

probe.question: What causes a spark when you take off a woollen sweater in the dark?
probe.wrong_answer: Friction heats the air to make fire.

misconceptions.root_belief: familiar effect of an action explains every outcome

misconceptions.statement: Lightning is made by clouds colliding like hard objects.
misconceptions.why: Thunder sounds like collision, so students picture clouds crashing.
misconceptions.fix: Clouds get charged by rubbing of ice and water particles. Lightning is the discharge between clouds or cloud and ground.

probe.question: What makes lightning in the sky?
probe.wrong_answer: Clouds bump into each other and spark.

misconceptions.root_belief: big events need big visible collisions
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas of weather and lightning

misconceptions.statement: A lightning conductor attracts lightning and so makes buildings less safe.
misconceptions.why: Students think a pointed metal rod invites danger.
misconceptions.fix: It gives lightning an easy path through a thick metal strip to the ground, so the building is not damaged.

probe.question: Why is a metal rod fixed on top of a tall building?
probe.wrong_answer: To attract lightning to the building.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Charge flows from a charged object to another only if they touch through a wire.
misconceptions.why: Students only see electric flow in circuits with wires.
misconceptions.fix: Charge can flow through any conductor, including the human body and moist air.

probe.question: Can a charged rod lose charge when touched by a person?
probe.wrong_answer: No, there is no wire.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the familiar form of a process counts
